title: POC weekly sync - throughput optimization
summary: Weekly POC sync to review throughput benchmarks, tuning changes (continuous batching, concurrency targets, queueing) and agree next steps. Redwood SE reviewed the overnight runs, continuous batching gave 2.3x throughput improvement on the H100 nodes, latency tradeoffs discussed, queueing/backpressure and concurrency caps to avoid tail latency spikes. Agreed action items: share updated batching config & cost sim, run 24h production-like soak with concurrency cap=150, schedule deep dive on queuing implementation.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-03
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Oliver Park (Redwood SE), Sofia Lopez (Redwood CSM), Raj Patel (NovaPay), Lina Gomez (NovaPay infra), Tom Hsu (NovaPay CTO)

[00:00] Maya: Hey team, thanks for joining, quick agenda — run through the overnight benchmark, talk through tuning we made for continuous batching and then agree soak plan. Lina, you good on time?
[00:08] Lina: Yup all good, we pulled overnight logs and some of the traces.
[00:12] Oliver: Cool, I'll start with results. Quick reminder: we ran the workload on the H100 cluster you gave us access to, 8 GPU nodes, same model config as last week but with the continuous batching patch enabled plus a slightly higher max batch size.
[00:25] Oliver: Baseline (no cont-batch) was about 3.2k tokens/sec aggregate, p95 240ms, p99 420ms under 120 concurrency. With continuous batching enabled we saw aggregate go to ~7.4k tokens/sec — roughly 2.3x — and p95 latency moved to ~320ms, p99 540ms. So throughput improved but tail latency ticked up.
[00:47] Raj: That matches what we saw in our quick spot checks. Can you clarify what you mean by continuous batching? Are you batching across requests that arrive within a short window or doing dynamic padding?
[00:59] Oliver: It's a combination — continuous batching aggregates inflight requests into the KV cache/pipeline and dispatches larger micro-batches more frequently rather than waiting for fixed window. There's also dynamic sequence bucketing so we don't pad everything to max length. The improvement comes from higher GPU utilization and better kernel throughput.
[01:18] Tom: Any changes needed on our side? We run a k8s autoscaler and our frontend gateway currently allows bursts up to 400 concurrent requests; we were worried that increasing concurrency would blow up tail latency.
[01:29] Sofia: Yeah that's exactly the tradeoff we saw — if you drive concurrency too high you get more batching and higher throughput but also more head-of-line contention and queueing which raises p99.
[01:40] Oliver: Right — our recommendation: pick a target concurrency that balances your latency SLOs. For NovaPay you mentioned 95% of calls need <350ms, and p99 ideally under 700ms. With cont-batch we can hit your throughput goals at concurrency=150 with p95 ~300ms and p99 ~580ms in our runs. At concurrency=300 the throughput is higher but p99 jumps above 800ms.
[02:07] Raj: Good to know. The team cares about cost too — can you share a cost simulation showing tokens/second vs $/hr for both cont-batch and baseline?
[02:16] Maya: Yes we'll send a cost sim. The continuous batching path is more GPU-efficient so cost per-token goes down, but there is that latency tail tradeoff which might require more capacity to respect SLOs. We'll put both in the spreadsheet.
[02:28] Lina: We also observed some retries from our gateway around 03:00 UTC during the soak, there were a few spikes where the frontend retried because it had built-in short timeouts. That amplified the load and created transient queue pressure.
[02:40] Oliver: Good find. Retries at the frontend will indeed amplify tail risk. Two mitigations: 1) add client-side jitter and backoff, reduce aggressive retry policy; 2) put a concurrency cap at the gateway or at the Redwood route level so the system sheds load gracefully.
[02:55] Tom: Does Redwood support per-route concurrency caps or token bucket queueing today?
[02:59] Oliver: Yes, we've got per-route inflight limits and you can configure queueing behavior: max inflight, queue depth, and max wait. We also have a fallback policy — if queue depth is exceeded we can fail fast or route to a smaller/faster model variant.
[03:14] Raj: Can you give an example config? Like what's the format and recommended numbers?
[03:19] Oliver: Example: max_inflight: 150, queue_depth: 300, max_wait_ms: 250, fallback_model: gpt-2-smaller (or a quantized variant). For NovaPay we recommended starting at 150 inflight.
[03:31] Maya: We'll include that example in the config we send. Also note we reduced max_batch_size from 32 to 24 during the run to help with tail behavior — that kept throughput high but reduced p99 a bit.
[03:44] Lina: Do you have metrics for GPU utilization and kernel occupancy? That would help us correlate.
[03:49] Oliver: Yup — we captured GPU util ~88% avg with cont-batch, kernel occupancy improved by 20% on the heavy attention kernels. We'll attach the dashboard and a raw csv.
[04:01] Raj: Any concerns about KV cache invalidation or correctness when batching across sessions? We have stateful chat sessions.
[04:07] Oliver: We respect KV cache per session; continuous batching merges requests only when session ids differ, but it keeps per-session KV integrity. There were some edge cases with very long sequences where memory pressure caused small evictions — we flagged them and patched the cache allocator; we'll include notes.
[04:23] Tom: For the soak test we plan to emulate production mix — 60% short queries (avg 40 tokens), 30% medium (150 tokens), 10% long (600+ tokens). Does that mix sound okay?
[04:34] Oliver: Yes that's a representative mix. For long sequences continuous batching helps less because padding overhead is larger, but the dynamic bucketing did help.
[04:41] Raj: On the cost side, what's the expected change per 100M tokens?
[04:45] Maya: Quick ballpark from the sim: baseline $X per 100M tokens on H100; cont-batch reduces cost by ~28% given same delivered throughput. We'll include exact numbers in the sheet.
[04:57] Lina: We also need to validate autoscaler behavior — when queue builds up does the autoscaler spin up too many pods? We use KEDA with custom metrics.
[05:05] Oliver: We recommend treating the queue depth as a signal but smoothing it — don't autoscale directly on instantaneous queue. Use a 1-3 minute window and a cap on scale velocity so you don't get cascading effects. We'll add recommended autoscaler knobs.
[05:18] Sofia: Ok, let's recap and assign next steps.
[05:21] Maya: Action items: we'll send the updated batching config + cost sim, include GPU util dashboards, example queueing config, and fallback model suggestions. NovaPay will run the 24h soak with concurrency cap 150 and share logs. We'll schedule an ops-level deep dive next Tuesday to go over queueing and autoscaler settings.
[05:40] Raj: Sounds good. One last Q — any security or audit implications when enabling continuous batching? Logs, request attribution?
[05:47] Oliver: No changes to auth — every request is still logged at the token/request level and appears in the audit trail. The only difference is some internal aggregation of requests for batching, but we keep request-level attribution intact for billing and audit. We'll share a short note and sample audit extract.
[06:05] Tom: Great, thanks everyone.
[06:07] Maya: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the artifacts.

Nota bene: Transcript contains occasional mis-transcriptions (e.g., "K V cache" vs KV-cache, product names abbreviated). Links mentioned during call: https://redwood.ai/docs/batching-config (sample), https://redwood.ai/dashboards/novapay-benchmark (dashboard link - provided after call).
